config.title: Form Library from Scratch

intro.title: Form Library from Scratch
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple form library from scratch using React and TypeScript. You'll learn how to create a reusable form component that manages its own state and handles user input. The core concept is controlled components, where form elements like inputs are directly tied to React state. You'll use TypeScript to define types for form values and event handlers, ensuring type safety. By the end, you'll have a custom form component that can be easily reused in your projects.
intro.usecase: Building a custom form library is a common task for React developers working on large-scale applications like admin dashboards, e-commerce platforms, or SaaS products. For example, a dashboard for managing user accounts might have complex forms for profile editing, data filtering, and settings configuration, all requiring consistent validation, state management, and submission handling. By creating a reusable library, developers can ensure uniform behavior across forms, reduce repetitive code, and maintain better control over performance and accessibility. This pattern is essential for teams that need to enforce design systems or integrate with specific backend APIs without relying on third-party solutions.

objectives: Implement a custom form state management hook using TypeScript interfaces
Construct reusable form input components with controlled value binding
Apply validation rules to form fields and display error messages
Initialize form data structures and handle submission events
Render dynamic form layouts with proper TypeScript typing
Manipulate form state through controlled input handlers
Integrate form validation logic with user interaction feedback

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and the useState hook.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing modules for a project
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are available for use in your form library.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and useState from 'react' to proceed.

steps.title: Define FormValues interface
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named FormValues with two string properties: name and email.
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Define FormValues interface here
steps.expectedOutcome: An interface FormValues is defined with name and email as string properties.
successCriteria: FormValues interface is defined with name: string and email: string properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure FormValues has both name and email properties, both typed as strings.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Check that you used 'interface FormValues' with the required string properties.

steps.title: Create main FormComponent
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named FormComponent that returns a simple <form> element with no content yet.
steps.hint: Define a component that returns JSX. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.expectedOutcome: A FormComponent function is defined that returns an empty <form> element.
successCriteria: FormComponent is defined as a function
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main form component structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're returning a <form> element from your component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Try creating a function named FormComponent that returns a <form> element.

steps.title: Initialize form state with useState
steps.instruction: Inside your FormComponent, initialize a state variable called formData using useState with the FormValues type. Provide an initial value that matches the FormValues interface structure.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. The initial value should be an object with properties matching the FormValues interface (e.g., name, email).
steps.expectedOutcome: The formData state variable is properly typed with FormValues and initialized with default values.
successCriteria: formData state is declared using useState with FormValues type and has a valid initial object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure formData uses the FormValues type and has a complete initial object.
steps.feedbackWrong: The formData state isn't properly initialized. Check that you're using useState with the FormValues type and providing initial values.

steps.title: Create handleChange function
steps.instruction: Inside your FormComponent, define a handleChange function that takes an event parameter and updates the formData state using the input's name and value.
steps.hint: The function should use setFormData to update only the specific field that changed. You can access the input's name and value from event.target.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleChange function that properly updates the formData state when called with an input change event.
successCriteria: The handleChange function is defined inside FormComponent, takes an event parameter, and updates formData using setFormData with the correct field name and value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function properly accesses event.target.name and event.target.value, and uses setFormData to update the specific field.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleChange function should update the formData state based on the input's name and value. Check that you're using setFormData correctly.

steps.title: Create handleSubmit function
steps.instruction: Inside your FormComponent, define a function named handleSubmit that takes a React.FormEvent parameter, prevents the default form submission, and logs the current formData to the console.
steps.hint: The function should accept an event parameter, call event.preventDefault(), then console.log(formData).
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have a handleSubmit function ready to be connected to a form's onSubmit event.
successCriteria: A handleSubmit function is defined that prevents default form submission and logs formData.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but make sure it prevents default form submission and logs the formData.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleSubmit function isn't defined correctly. Check that it accepts a FormEvent parameter and logs the formData.

steps.title: Add form container element
steps.instruction: In the FormComponent's return statement, replace the current null with a <form> element that has an onSubmit attribute wired to the handleSubmit function.
steps.hint: The form element should wrap around where your form fields will go later. Use the onSubmit prop to connect it to your existing handleSubmit function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a form element with the onSubmit handler properly connected, creating the basic structure for your form library.
successCriteria: The component returns a <form> element with an onSubmit attribute set to handleSubmit.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're returning a <form> element with the onSubmit attribute set to handleSubmit. Check that you've replaced the null return value.
steps.feedbackWrong: return a <form> element from the component and connect it to the handleSubmit function using the onSubmit attribute.

steps.title: Add name input field
steps.instruction: Inside the form container element, add an input field for the name property. Set its type to 'text', name to 'name', value to formData.name, and onChange to handleChange.
steps.hint: Create a standard HTML input element with the appropriate attributes. Remember to bind the value to formData.name and the onChange event to your handleChange function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The form will contain a text input field for the name property, with proper TypeScript binding to the form state.
successCriteria: Input element exists inside the form
Input value is bound to formData.name
Input onChange is bound to handleChange
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure the input has all required attributes: type='text', name='name', value={formData.name}, and onChange={handleChange}.
steps.feedbackWrong: The name input field is missing or incomplete. Check that you've added an input element with the correct attributes inside the form.

steps.title: Add email input field
steps.instruction: Inside the form, add an email input field below the existing name input. The email input should have: type='email', name='email', value={formData.email}, and onChange={handleChange}.
steps.hint: Add a new <input> element with the required attributes. Make sure the name attribute matches the property name in your FormValues interface.
steps.expectedOutcome: The form will have two controlled input fields: one for name and one for email. Both inputs will update the formData state when typed into.
successCriteria: An email input field is added with type='email', name='email', value={formData.email}, and onChange={handleChange} attributes.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added an input, but check that all required attributes are present: type='email', name='email', value={formData.email}, and onChange={handleChange}.
steps.feedbackWrong: The email input field is missing or incomplete. Make sure to add an <input> element with all the required attributes.

steps.title: Add submit button
steps.instruction: Inside the form element, add a submit button with the text 'Submit'.
steps.hint: Use the <button> element with type='submit' attribute to create a submit button.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding a submit button to a form
<form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
  <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>
steps.expectedOutcome: The form now includes a submit button that triggers the handleSubmit function when clicked.
successCriteria: A submit button element with type='submit' and text 'Submit' is added inside the form element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a button, but make sure it has type='submit' and the text 'Submit'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The submit button is missing or incorrect. Add a <button type="submit">Submit</button> inside the form.
